etymology: From Anglo-Saxon setl, a seat, and setlan, to place or seat. Webster 1828: to place in a fixed state; to establish; to fix; and as a noun, a seat or bench — the sense the Authorized Version keeps for the ledge of Ezekiel’s altar.
biblical_def: Our Lord’s counsel to disciples facing tribunals is that the decision be made long before the summons: Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to meditate before what ye shall answer (Luke 21:14). The settling is of a resolve, not of a speech; He forbids rehearsal precisely because He promises to give a mouth and wisdom in the hour. Peter ends his epistle with the word as the last of four verbs, and the order is a summary of the Christian life: the God of all grace... after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you (1 Peter 5:10). Note where suffering stands — before the settling, not after it, and as the means rather than the obstacle. The word is also a noun in the older English. Ezekiel measures the altar by its ledges: from the bottom upon the ground even to the lower settle shall be two cubits... and from the lesser settle even to the greater settle shall be four cubits (Ezekiel 43:14). And God is said to settle the ground itself: Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers (Psalm 65:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SETTLE as to place in a fixed or permanent condition; to establish; to confirm; to fix; to quiet or compose; and as a noun, a seat, a bench, a place to sit on.
webster_full: SETTLE, n. — A seat or bench; something to sit on.
SETTLE, v.t. — To place in a fixed or permanent condition; to make firm or stable; to establish.
To fix or establish; to confirm; as, to settle the succession.
To quiet; to compose; to still; as, to settle the mind after agitation.
To adjust; to determine; to close, as an account or a controversy. Anglo-Saxon setl, a seat.
scriptures: Luke 21:14
Settle it therefore in your hearts, not to meditate before what ye shall answer:
1 Peter 5:10
But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you.
Ezekiel 43:14

And from the bottom upon the ground even to the lower settle shall be two cubits, and the breadth one cubit; and from the lesser settle even to the greater settle shall be four cubits, and the breadth one cubit.
Psalm 65:10
Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof.
corruption_summary: 1 Peter 5:10 makes suffering the appointed road to a settled soul, which is the opposite of the assumption that affliction is an interruption to be explained away or escaped.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter’s sentence has an order that will not be rearranged: after that ye have suffered a while comes first, and then the four verbs — perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle. Suffering is not the obstacle to the settling; it is the means God uses. Two errors run against this from opposite sides. Prosperity teaching treats affliction as a sign of insufficient faith and therefore as something the believer should be able to cancel; the therapeutic instinct treats it as damage whose only meaning is to be recovered from. Scripture treats it as fatherly discipline that yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to them that are exercised thereby (Hebrews 12:11). The 1689 Confession accordingly speaks of God’s wise and holy providence leaving His children for a season to manifold temptations and the corruptions of their own hearts, to humble them and to raise them to a closer dependence on Him.

Luke 21:14 is worth pressing because our Lord forbids something that looks like prudence. Disciples on trial are told not to meditate before what ye shall answer — not to prepare the speech — while being told to settle the resolve in advance. The distinction is exact and pastorally useful: the Christian is to fix beforehand that he will confess Christ, and to leave the wording to the Spirit in the hour. This is not a warrant against study or preparation generally; the same Lord commands His people to be ready always to give an answer (1 Peter 3:15). It is a promise attached to a specific extremity, and the martyrs of the Reformation and after have repeatedly found it kept.
roots_summary: Greek tithemi (G5087), to place or fix, in the phrase settle in your hearts; themelioo (G2311), to lay a foundation, to settle; Hebrew azarah (H5835), a ledge or enclosure; nachath (H5181), to settle down.

After that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you (1 Peter 5:10) — suffering stands before the settling, as its means.
From the lesser settle even to the greater settle (Ezekiel 43:14) — the older English noun, a ledge of the altar.

etymology: From Latin supponere, to put under, to substitute, through French supposer. Webster 1828: to lay down or state as a proposition or fact that may exist; to imagine; to think. Our Lord repeatedly uses it to introduce an assumption He is about to demolish.
biblical_def: Suppose ye is one of Christ’s standing formulas for exposing a comfortable assumption. The hardest instance is His own account of what He came to do: Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division (Luke 12:51). The peace He gives is peace with God (Romans 5:1), and its arrival in a fallen household divides it — a fact the following verses spell out family member by family member. He uses the same construction of the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled and the eighteen on whom the tower fell, and in both cases the answer is Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:3). The word also marks honest human estimation. Peter corrects a crowd’s hasty reading of Pentecost: these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day (Acts 2:15). And John closes his Gospel with a supposition offered as reverent hyperbole: I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written (John 21:25).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUPPOSE as to lay down or state as a proposition or fact that may exist or be true, though not known or believed to be true; to imagine; to think; to receive as true.
webster_full: SUPPOSE, v.t. — To lay down or state as a proposition or fact that may exist or be true, though not known or believed to be so.
To imagine; to believe; to receive as true.
To imply; to admit as previously existing; as, the effect supposes a cause.
To think; to be of opinion; as, I suppose it to be so.
Latin supponere, from sub, under, and pono, to put — to place under as a ground of reasoning.
scriptures: Luke 12:51
Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division:
Luke 13:3
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
Acts 2:15
For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day.
John 21:25
And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.
corruption_summary: Luke 12:51 is Christ denying in His own words the sentimental portrait of Him as a teacher of universal harmony, and it is among the most consistently avoided verses in modern preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division. The verse is not a qualification of the gospel of peace but an honest statement of its effect in a world at enmity with God. Christ is the Prince of Peace and reconciles sinners to the Father; that same reconciliation sets the reconciled at odds with those who refuse it, and the following verses in Luke 12 name the fault lines as running through the household itself. The sentimental Jesus of modern religious imagination — affirming, inclusive, chiefly concerned with harmony — cannot say this sentence, which is why it is so seldom read. Where the church adopts that portrait, it loses the ability to call anything sin, since the calling would produce the division the portrait was constructed to avoid.

Luke 13:3 shows the same formula turned on a favourite instinct: the assumption that catastrophe indicates worse-than-ordinary guilt in its victims. Christ denies it flatly, and then refuses to leave the questioners comfortable — except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Both halves must be kept. The first forbids reading providence as a scoreboard, which is the error of Job’s comforters and of every modern pronouncement that a disaster was judgment on the people who suffered it. The second forbids concluding that because the victims were no worse, the survivors are safe. Scripture’s use of catastrophe is not diagnostic of the dead but hortatory to the living.
roots_summary: Greek dokeo (G1380), to think or suppose; nomizo (G3543), to hold by custom, to suppose; hupolambano (G5274), to take up, to assume; oimai (G3633), to expect or suppose.
roots_lines: Greek dokeo (G1380) — to think, to seem, to suppose; Suppose ye that I am come to give peace? (Luke 12:51).
Greek hupolambano (G5274) — to take up, and so to assume; as ye suppose (Acts 2:15).
Greek oimai (G3633) — to suppose or expect; John’s closing estimate (John 21:25).
Greek nomizo (G3543) — to suppose by custom or convention; used of mistaken assumptions throughout Acts.
Greek diamerismos (G1267) — division, dissension; what Christ says He came to bring (Luke 12:51).
usage: Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay (Luke 12:51) — Christ denying the sentimental portrait in His own words.
Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:3) — catastrophe is hortatory to the living, not diagnostic of the dead.
These are not drunken, as ye suppose (Acts 2:15) — a crowd’s hasty reading corrected by the hour of the day.

etymology: From Latin copia, plenty, abundance — a transcript being a multiplying of the original. Webster 1828: a transcript from an original; an imitation or resemblance. Deuteronomy requires a king to make one with his own hand, and the requirement is a doctrine of government.
biblical_def: The law of the king in Deuteronomy is remarkable for what it commands a monarch to do personally: when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites (Deuteronomy 17:18). Not commission a copy — write one. The following verses say it shall be with him and he shall read therein all the days of his life, that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren. The sovereign is placed under a text he has transcribed by hand. Joshua carries out the public counterpart on Ebal: he wrote there upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel (Joshua 8:32). Copying is likewise how the wisdom literature reached us: These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out (Proverbs 25:1) — a note preserved in the canon about the canon’s own transmission. And Ezra’s opponents send their accusation in the same form: This is the copy of the letter that they sent unto him, even unto Artaxerxes the king (Ezra 4:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines COPY as a transcript from an original writing; an imitation, likeness or reproduction; a pattern or example to be imitated.
webster_full: COPY, n. — A transcript from an original writing; hence, a writing like another.
An imitation, likeness or reproduction of an original.
A pattern; an example proposed for imitation; as, a copy set for a learner.
COPY, v.t. — To write, print or engrave according to an original; to transcribe; to imitate.
Latin copia, plenty — a transcript multiplying the original.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 17:18
And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites:
Joshua 8:32
And he wrote there upon the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he wrote in the presence of the children of Israel.
Proverbs 25:1
These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.
Deuteronomy 17:19
And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 17:18-19 places the highest civil authority under a written law he must copy and read for life, which is the biblical root of limited government and the standing answer to every claim of absolute sovereignty.
corruption_paragraphs: The king of Israel is not the source of law; he is a reader of it, and he is required to produce the text in his own handwriting so that no distance can open between the ruler and the rule. The purpose clause is explicit — that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren — which makes this the earliest statement of a principle later Reformed political thought would develop at length: authority is delegated, bounded, and answerable to a higher law it did not make. Samuel Rutherford’s Lex Rex argues the case from precisely such texts, against the divine right of kings as an absolute claim, and the Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate follows from it. This dictionary affirms the lordship of Christ over every sphere and the classical two-kingdoms distinction while rejecting the Radical Two-Kingdoms position that would remove God’s law from the magistrate’s horizon altogether.

Proverbs 25:1 is a small verse with a large use: the canon itself records that Hezekiah’s men copied out an earlier collection. Scripture is not embarrassed by its own transmission, and the modern habit of treating the existence of copyists and collections as evidence against inspiration mistakes the doctrine. Verbal plenary inspiration attaches to the original autographs; providential preservation is what has carried the text to us through exactly such labour as Hezekiah’s men performed. The 1689 Confession states both together — the Scriptures were immediately inspired by God, and by His singular care and providence kept pure in all ages. A copy faithfully made is not a diluted original; it is how the original reaches the reader.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishneh (H4932), a double or copy; parshegen (H6572), a copy or transcript; Greek antigraphon, a copy; the Septuagint’s rendering of mishneh here gave the book of Deuteronomy its name.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishneh (H4932) — a double, a second, a copy; a copy of this law (Deuteronomy 17:18) and on the stones at Ebal (Joshua 8:32).
Greek deuteronomion — the second law, the Septuagint’s rendering of mishneh hattorah, which supplied the English name of the book.
Hebrew parshegen (H6572) — a copy or transcript of a document; the copy of the letter (Ezra 4:11).
Hebrew athaq (H6275) — to move or transcribe; which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out (Proverbs 25:1).
Hebrew torah (H8451) — the law, the thing copied and read all the days of the king’s life.
usage: He shall write him a copy of this law in a book (Deuteronomy 17:18) — not commission a copy; write one.
That he may learn to fear the LORD his God (Deuteronomy 17:19) — the sovereign placed under a text by his own hand.
Which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out (Proverbs 25:1) — the canon recording its own transmission.

etymology: From Old French dresser, to arrange or set in order, from Latin directiare, to make straight. Webster 1828: to adjust; to put in good order; to trim or cultivate, as a vineyard; to prepare, as food. The Authorized Version rarely uses it of clothing; it means tending and preparing.
biblical_def: The first commission given to man is a gardener’s: the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it (Genesis 2:15). Work precedes the fall. Adam is set to cultivate and to guard before there is any curse, thorn or sweat, which settles the question of whether labour is a punishment: it is not, though Genesis 3 makes it hard. The word belongs to vineyards, and Deuteronomy uses it in a covenant curse whose sting is futility rather than idleness: Thou shalt plant vineyards, and dress them, but shalt neither drink of the wine, nor gather the grapes; for the worms shall eat them (Deuteronomy 28:39). It also means preparing a beast for sacrifice or a meal for a guest. Elijah proposes the terms on Carmel with it: let them choose one bullock for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay it on wood, and put no fire under: and I will dress the other bullock (1 Kings 18:23). And Nathan’s parable turns on the rich man who would not take of his own flock to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him (2 Samuel 12:4).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DRESS as to adjust; to put in good order; to trim, cultivate and prepare, as a vineyard or a field; to prepare, as food for the table; and secondarily to clothe.
webster_full: DRESS, v.t. — To make straight or a straight line; to adjust to a right line.
To put in good order; to trim; to cultivate; as, to dress a vineyard or a garden.
To prepare, as food, for the table; to cook.
To clothe; to invest with garments or habiliments.
Old French dresser, from Latin directiare, to make straight — the same root as direct and address.
scriptures: Genesis 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Deuteronomy 28:39
Thou shalt plant vineyards, and dress them, but shalt neither drink of the wine, nor gather the grapes; for the worms shall eat them.
1 Kings 18:23

Let them therefore give us two bullocks; and let them choose one bullock for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay it on wood, and put no fire under: and I will dress the other bullock, and lay it on wood, and put no fire under:
2 Samuel 12:4

And there came a traveller unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him; but took the poor man's lamb, and dressed it for the man that was come to him.
corruption_summary: Genesis 2:15 puts labour in the garden before the fall, which contradicts both the notion that work is a curse and the notion that the creation mandate has been retired.
corruption_paragraphs: Adam is given work in an unfallen world. The dressing and keeping of the garden belongs to man’s original condition, not to his punishment, and Genesis 3 adds thorns, sweat and futility to a task that already existed. This settles two errors at once. The first is the common assumption — more felt than argued — that labour is inherently the curse, from which the Christian hope is escape into rest; Scripture’s hope is redeemed work, and Revelation 22:3 says His servants shall serve Him. The second is the retreat that treats the creation mandate of Genesis 1:28 as superseded by the Great Commission. It is not superseded; it is carried forward under the lordship of Christ over every sphere, which is why vocation, cultivation and dominion remain Christian categories. The Reformers recovered exactly this against the medieval elevation of the contemplative life over ordinary calling.

Deuteronomy 28:39 names a curse the modern reader feels immediately: not the absence of work but its futility. A man plants, dresses, tends, and eats nothing. Ecclesiastes explores the same vanity at length, and the New Testament answers it not by denying the futility but by locating the exception: your labour is not in vain in the Lord (1 Corinthians 15:58), placed deliberately at the end of the resurrection chapter. The believer’s work is not preserved from thorns in this age; it is preserved from meaninglessness by the resurrection. Any account of Christian vocation that promises the first has promised what Deuteronomy 28 says God may withhold.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, guard, watch over; the paired command and to keep it (Genesis 2:15).
Hebrew asah (H6213) — to make, to prepare; used of dressing a beast for sacrifice or a meal (1 Kings 18:23; 2 Samuel 12:4).
Hebrew kerem (H3754) — a vineyard; the standing object of dressing in the law and prophets.
Hebrew nata (H5193) — to plant; joined to dressing in the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:39.
usage: To dress it and to keep it (Genesis 2:15) — work given to man before any curse, thorn or sweat.
Thou shalt plant vineyards, and dress them, but shalt neither drink of the wine (Deuteronomy 28:39) — the curse is futility, not idleness.
I will dress the other bullock, and lay it on wood, and put no fire under (1 Kings 18:23) — Elijah setting the terms on Carmel.

etymology: From Latin miscere, to mingle. Webster 1828: united or blended promiscuously in a mass or compound. Scripture uses it of the crowd that left Egypt with Israel, and of the faith that must be blended with preaching if preaching is to profit.
biblical_def: The exodus did not carry a pure company: And a mixed multitude went up also with them; and flocks, and herds, even very much cattle (Exodus 12:38). This crowd reappears at the worst moments — it is the mixed multitude that fell a lusting in Numbers 11:4 and drew Israel after them — and Nehemiah records the eventual separation: when they had heard the law, that they separated from Israel all the mixed multitude (Nehemiah 13:3). A visible community may always contain more than the true people of God, and the law read aloud is what distinguishes them. The most searching use is in Hebrews, where the same gospel produces opposite results: unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it (Hebrews 4:2). Hearing is not the variable; the wilderness generation heard. Faith is. And Daniel sees an empire whose weakness is precisely its composition, partly strong, and partly broken, the iron mixed with miry clay (Daniel 2:41-42).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MIXED as united or blended in a mass or compound; formed by mixture; promiscuous; consisting of various kinds or of different elements.
webster_full: MIX, v.t. — To unite or blend promiscuously two or more ingredients into a mass or compound.
To join; to associate; to unite with in company.
MIXED, pp. — United in a mass or compound; blended; promiscuous.
MIXTURE, n. — The act of mixing; a mass or compound consisting of different ingredients blended without order.
Latin misceo, to mix — the root of miscellaneous and promiscuous.
scriptures: Exodus 12:38
And a mixed multitude went up also with them; and flocks, and herds, even very much cattle.
Nehemiah 13:3
Now it came to pass, when they had heard the law, that they separated from Israel all the mixed multitude.
Hebrews 4:2
For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.
Daniel 2:41

And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters' clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 4:2 locates the difference between a profited and an unprofited hearer entirely in faith, which is fatal both to sacramentalism and to the assumption that exposure to preaching is itself saving.
corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness generation had the same gospel preached to them and it did not profit them, not being mixed with faith. This single clause rules out any scheme in which the means of grace operate by their own performance. Rome’s doctrine that the sacraments confer grace ex opere operato — by the work worked — is the most systematic form of the error, but it has an evangelical counterpart wherever regular attendance under sound preaching is treated as itself a ground of hope. Scripture makes faith the appointed instrument, and faith is God’s gift (Ephesians 2:8), not a contribution that turns a general benefit into a personal one. The Reformed doctrine of the means of grace holds both halves: the word and ordinances are the appointed channels, and they profit only where the Spirit gives faith to receive them.

The mixed multitude is the Old Testament picture behind the Reformed distinction between the visible and the invisible church. Israel came out of Egypt with a crowd attached, and that crowd is named at the point of the worst rebellion. Our Lord teaches the same in the parables of the tares and the net: the visible assembly contains both until the harvest, and the servants are not to attempt a final sorting. This is not indifference to church purity — Nehemiah 13:3 shows a lawful separation, and the New Testament requires discipline — but it forbids the sectarian ambition of a perfectly pure membership, which has wrecked more than one movement. The 1689 Confession accordingly speaks of the purest churches under heaven as subject to mixture and error.

Hebrew asaphsuph (H628) — a collected rabble; the mixt multitude of Numbers 11:4.
Greek sugkerannumi (G4786) — to mix together, to blend into one; not being mixed with faith (Hebrews 4:2).
Aramaic arab (H6151) — to mingle; the iron mixed with miry clay (Daniel 2:41).
Greek opheleo (G5623) — to profit or benefit; what the word failed to do without faith (Hebrews 4:2).
usage: A mixed multitude went up also with them (Exodus 12:38) — the redeemed company had a crowd attached from the first day.
Not being mixed with faith in them that heard it (Hebrews 4:2) — hearing is not the variable; faith is.
They separated from Israel all the mixed multitude (Nehemiah 13:3) — and the law read aloud is what distinguished them.

etymology: From Old French avis, opinion, from Latin ad visum, according to what is seen. Webster 1828: counsel; an opinion recommended or offered as worthy to be followed. Scripture records advice taken and advice refused, and hangs the fate of a kingdom on one of each.
biblical_def: Rehoboam’s reign was decided by whose advice he preferred: And answered them after the advice of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add thereto: my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions (2 Chronicles 10:14). He had already heard the old men, who told him that if he would be a servant to the people they would be his servants for ever, and he forsook it. Ten tribes went with the answer. Against that stands David’s response to Abigail, one of the few places in Scripture where a man blesses the counsel that stopped him: blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand (1 Samuel 25:33). Proverbs makes advice a condition of prudent war: Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war (Proverbs 20:18). And the men of Israel, confronted with the outrage at Gibeah, call for it before acting: Behold, ye are all children of Israel; give here your advice and counsel (Judges 20:7) — though the sequel shows that taking advice is no guarantee of taking it wisely.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ADVICE as counsel; an opinion recommended, or offered as worthy to be followed; also information, notice, or intelligence given.
webster_full: ADVICE, n. — Counsel; an opinion recommended, or offered as worthy to be followed.
Prudent deliberation; consideration; as, to act with advice.
Information; notice; intelligence; as, advices from abroad.
ADVISE, v.t. — To give counsel to; to offer an opinion as worthy or expedient to be followed.
Old French avis, from Latin ad visum, according to what is seen or appears.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 10:14
And answered them after the advice of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add thereto: my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.
1 Samuel 25:33
And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand.
Proverbs 20:18
Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.
Judges 20:7
Behold, ye are all children of Israel; give here your advice and counsel.
corruption_summary: 1 Samuel 25 has a woman’s counsel restrain the LORD’s anointed and David bless her for it, which neither the egalitarian reading nor the caricature of complementarianism handles honestly.
corruption_paragraphs: Abigail intercepts David on his way to slaughter Nabal’s household, reasons with him from the LORD’s purpose for him, and David blesses her advice and turns back. The passage is regularly enlisted by egalitarian argument as evidence against any creational order of headship, and it proves nothing of the sort: the order of headship and male eldership that this dictionary holds (Ephesians 5:22-33; 1 Timothy 2:11-15) concerns authority in the home and church, not the capacity of women to think, counsel, rebuke, or be right. But the passage is equally a rebuke to the caricature that some complementarian practice has produced, in which a man treats counsel from a woman as an intrusion on his headship. David was the LORD’s anointed, armed, and wrong; Abigail was neither his wife nor under his authority, and she was right. Scripture commends her for speaking and him for listening.

2 Chronicles 10 shows the other outcome and its mechanism. Rehoboam did not refuse advice; he collected it and then chose the counsel that flattered his estimate of himself. This is the ordinary form of the failure, and it is why Proverbs pairs counsel with humility so often — the way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise (Proverbs 12:15). The narrative also states the deeper cause: the turn of affairs was of God, that He might perform His word by Ahijah (2 Chronicles 10:15). Both are true at once, without contradiction and without excusing Rehoboam. That is the Reformed doctrine of concurrence — God’s decree accomplished through the free and culpable choices of men.
roots_summary: Hebrew etsah (H6098), counsel, advice, purpose; taam (H2940), taste, discretion, judgment; tachbulah (H8458), wise guidance, sound counsel.
roots_lines: Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, advice, plan; the word behind Rehoboam’s choice (2 Chronicles 10:14) and Abigail’s speech (1 Samuel 25:33).
Hebrew taam (H2940) — taste, and so discretion or judgment; the discernment Abigail is commended for.
Hebrew tachbulah (H8458) — steering, sound guidance, from the word for a ship’s ropes; with good advice make war (Proverbs 20:18).
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word or matter; give here your advice and counsel (Judges 20:7).
Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to advise or counsel; the verb from which etsah is formed.
usage: Answered them after the advice of the young men (2 Chronicles 10:14) — he collected counsel and chose the flattering kind.
Blessed be thy advice... which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood (1 Samuel 25:33) — the LORD’s anointed, armed and wrong, blessing the counsel that stopped him.
With good advice make war (Proverbs 20:18) — deliberation as a condition of lawful action.

etymology: From Old French estoffe, material, furniture, goods. Webster 1828: substance or matter indefinitely; furniture; goods; domestic vessels. The Authorized Version uses it for a man’s movable belongings, and our Lord makes it the thing not to go back for.
biblical_def: In the warning about the day of the Son of man, one clause decides between escape and ruin: In that day, he which shall be upon the housetop, and his stuff in the house, let him not come down to take it away: and he that is in the field, let him likewise not return back (Luke 17:31). The next verse is two words — Remember Lot’s wife. The stuff is not condemned; going back for it is. Jacob challenges Laban to produce evidence from his belongings: Whereas thou hast searched all my stuff, what hast thou found of all thy household stuff? set it here before my brethren and thy brethren, that they may judge betwixt us both (Genesis 31:37). The word supplies one of the strangest scenes in the Old Testament, when Israel’s first king cannot be found at his own coronation: they enquired of the LORD further, if the man should yet come thither. And the LORD answered, Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff (1 Samuel 10:22). And at the tabernacle the offerings finally exceeded the need: the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much (Exodus 36:7).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STUFF as substance or matter indefinitely; the matter of which anything is formed; furniture; goods; domestic vessels; and, in the older usage, a man’s movable belongings.
webster_full: STUFF, n. — Substance or matter indefinitely; the matter of which anything is formed.
Furniture; goods; domestic vessels; movables.
That which fills anything; as, the stuff of a bed.
Essence; elemental part; as, the very stuff of a man.
Old French estoffe, material; the same root as stow and stuff, v.
scriptures: Luke 17:31
In that day, he which shall be upon the housetop, and his stuff in the house, let him not come down to take it away: and he that is in the field, let him likewise not return back.
Genesis 31:37
Whereas thou hast searched all my stuff, what hast thou found of all thy household stuff? set it here before my brethren and thy brethren, that they may judge betwixt us both.
1 Samuel 10:22
Therefore they enquired of the LORD further, if the man should yet come thither. And the LORD answered, Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff.
Exodus 36:7
For the stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much.
corruption_summary: Luke 17:31-32 does not condemn possessions but the backward look, which is a subtler test than the one asceticism sets and a harder one than prosperity teaching admits exists.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ does not tell the man on the housetop to have no stuff; He tells him not to go down for it, and then says Remember Lot’s wife (Luke 17:32). She was outside Sodom, moving, already spared, and she looked back. The test Scripture sets here is not the quantity of a man’s goods but the direction of his affection under summons, which cuts against two errors at once. Asceticism — the monastic instinct that treats renunciation of property as itself a higher spirituality — misplaces the problem in the objects; the Reformers rejected it and recovered the goodness of ordinary calling and lawful possession. Prosperity teaching commits the opposite error by denying that possessions pose any spiritual danger worth naming, when our Lord names it repeatedly and calls covetousness idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

1 Samuel 10:22 is quietly devastating and rarely preached: at the moment of his public elevation, Saul is found hiding among the baggage. The narrative offers it without comment, but the whole subsequent reign is latent in it. The man who hid among the stuff would later spare Agag and the best of the sheep because he feared the people (1 Samuel 15:24), and would consult a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor. What looks at first like modesty was a settled disposition to shrink from God’s appointment and to be governed by what others saw. Scripture’s doctrine of the heart is that such dispositions do not stay small; they mature into the sins that finally undo a man.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli (H3627), a vessel, implement, or article of property; melakah (H4399), work or the material of work; Greek skeuos (G4632), a vessel or article of goods.
roots_lines: Greek skeuos (G4632) — a vessel, implement, or article of household goods; his stuff in the house (Luke 17:31).
Hebrew keli (H3627) — a vessel, utensil, or piece of property; hid himself among the stuff (1 Samuel 10:22).
Hebrew melakah (H4399) — work, and the material for work; the stuff they had was sufficient (Exodus 36:7).
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house or household; all thy household stuff (Genesis 31:37).
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the disposition the backward look reveals (Colossians 3:5).
usage: His stuff in the house, let him not come down to take it away (Luke 17:31) — the stuff is not condemned; going back for it is.
He hath hid himself among the stuff (1 Samuel 10:22) — Israel’s first king missing from his own coronation.
The stuff they had was sufficient for all the work to make it, and too much (Exodus 36:7) — the one recorded occasion of an offering that had to be stopped.

etymology: From Old French sire, from Latin senior, elder. Webster 1828: a word of respect used in addresses to men. In the Gospels it renders the Greek kurios in its ordinary courteous sense — the same word that elsewhere means Lord, and the gap between the two is often the point.
biblical_def: Greeks at the feast approach an apostle with a request that has been the text of a thousand pulpit fronts: The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus (John 12:21). They address Philip courteously and ask for the only thing worth asking. The Samaritan woman uses the same word to a stranger at a well and does not yet know what she is saying: Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water? (John 4:11) — by the end of the chapter the courtesy has become confession. The Philippian jailor’s question is the plainest in Scripture: Sirs, what must I do to be saved? (Acts 16:30), and the answer given him is equally plain. John, overwhelmed in the Revelation, answers an elder’s question with a confession of ignorance that is also a submission: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SIR as a word of respect used in addresses to men, as Madam is to women; also the title of a knight or baronet; and in the plural, a mode of address to a company of men.
webster_full: SIR, n. — A word of respect used in addresses to men, as Madam is in addresses to women.
The title of a knight or baronet; as Sir Isaac Newton.
In the plural, SIRS, a mode of addressing a company of men.
Formerly a title of respect given to priests and to graduates of universities.
Old French sire, from Latin senior, elder — the same root as senator and senior.
scriptures: John 12:21
The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus.
John 4:11
The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?
Acts 16:30
And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?
Revelation 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
corruption_summary: The jailor’s question and its answer are the New Testament’s plainest statement of the way of salvation, and both the question and the answer are routinely made more complicated than Scripture makes them.
corruption_paragraphs: Sirs, what must I do to be saved? is asked by a man who has just felt an earthquake and drawn his sword on himself, and the apostolic answer is Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house (Acts 16:31). Nothing is added as a condition — no penance, no probation, no rite performed first. Rome’s sacramental system makes baptism the instrument of regeneration and adds the whole apparatus of merit and satisfaction; the answer to the jailor knows nothing of it. But the passage equally refuses the reduction that treats belief as bare assent, for the narrative goes straight on to the washing of the apostles’ stripes, the household’s baptism, and rejoicing — faith immediately producing what faith produces. Believing on the Lord Jesus Christ is trust in a Person, and the fruit follows in the same paragraph.

John 4:11 rewards attention to the single Greek word. Kurios can mean nothing more than sir, and that is all the woman means at the well; by John 4:19 she calls Him a prophet, and by 4:29 she is asking whether this is the Christ. The Authorized Version’s rendering preserves the distance she still has to travel, and it is a useful corrective to the assumption that a person’s first words about Christ measure his final estimate of Him. Conversion in Scripture is often a lengthening of a title. It is also worth noting who receives this fullest self-disclosure of Messiah in the Gospels — a Samaritan woman with five husbands — which is the sovereign freedom of grace exercised exactly where respectable religion would not have looked.
roots_summary: Greek kurios (G2962), lord, master, sir; despotes (G1203), master or sovereign; Latin senior, elder, the source of the English word.
roots_lines: Greek kurios (G2962) — lord, master, and in ordinary courtesy sir; the same word rendered Lord of Christ throughout the New Testament.
Greek aner (G435) — a man; in the vocative plural it gives the jailor’s Sirs (Acts 16:30).
Greek despotes (G1203) — a master with absolute authority, used of God in Luke 2:29 and Acts 4:24.
Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to trust; the whole of the apostolic answer (Acts 16:31).
Latin senior — elder; through Old French sire into English sir.
usage: Sir, we would see Jesus (John 12:21) — courteous address, and the only request worth making.
Sirs, what must I do to be saved? (Acts 16:30) — the plainest question in Scripture, and the plainest answer.
Sir, thou knowest (Revelation 7:14) — a confession of ignorance that is also a submission.

etymology: From Old French trope, a band or company, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: a collection of people; a company; a body of soldiers. Jacob’s blessing on Gad turns on the word twice, and the second turn is the gospel of it.
biblical_def: The blessing of Gad is the shortest in Genesis 49 and one of the most quoted for encouragement: Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last (Genesis 49:19). The Hebrew plays on the tribe’s own name, and the shape of the sentence is the shape of the believer’s life — overcome first, overcoming at the last. Gad’s territory lay east of Jordan, exposed to raiders, and the blessing does not promise him exemption from them; it promises the end. David gives the same word a note of exultant strength, and credits it entirely to God: For by thee I have run through a troop: by my God have I leaped over a wall (2 Samuel 22:30). Job uses it of God Himself as the besieger, which is the hardest use in Scripture: His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle (Job 19:12). And Isaiah names a pagan deity of fortune whom Judah was courting with the same consonants: ye that forsake the LORD... that prepare a table for that troop, and that furnish the drink offering unto that number (Isaiah 65:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TROOP as a collection of people; a company; a number; a multitude; and specifically a body of soldiers, or a small body of cavalry.
webster_full: TROOP, n. — A collection of people; a company; a number; a multitude.
A body of soldiers; but applied to a small body or company of cavalry.
In the plural, TROOPS, soldiers in general; an army.
TROOP, v.i. — To collect in numbers; to march in a body or in haste.
Old French trope, a band; of Germanic origin, related to troupe.
scriptures: Genesis 49:19
Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last.
2 Samuel 22:30
For by thee I have run through a troop: by my God have I leaped over a wall.
His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle.
Isaiah 65:11
But ye are they that forsake the LORD, that forget my holy mountain, that prepare a table for that troop, and that furnish the drink offering unto that number.
corruption_summary: Genesis 49:19 promises Gad a final victory and no exemption from being overcome first, which is a truer account of the Christian life than either triumphalism or defeatism supplies.
corruption_paragraphs: A troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last. Both clauses are the blessing. Triumphalist preaching — whether the prosperity variety or the milder assumption that a walking Christian should be a winning one — keeps the second clause and quietly deletes the first, and leaves believers concluding from their defeats that something has gone wrong with their faith. Defeatism keeps the first and disbelieves the second. Scripture’s account is Gad’s: real reverses, and a certain end. Romans 8 has the same structure, listing tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril and sword as things actually encountered, and then calling believers more than conquerors in the midst of them, not instead of them. Perseverance of the saints is not the promise that the troop never overcomes; it is the promise about the last.

Isaiah 65:11 is worth naming because the corruption it describes is so recognisable. That troop and that number render Gad and Meni, deities of fortune and destiny, to whom Judah was setting a table while still claiming the LORD. This is not the replacement of God but the hedging of a bet — covenant religion maintained alongside a private arrangement with luck. The modern forms are not obscure: the horoscope kept for amusement, the manifesting vocabulary borrowed from the wider culture, the superstition about what one must or must not say aloud. The first commandment is not merely against choosing another god instead; it is against having any before Him, and the table prepared for fortune is the oldest way of breaking it while still attending the feast.
roots_summary: Hebrew gedud (H1416), a band, a raiding troop; gad (H1409), fortune, and the tribal name; meni (H4507), destiny or number.
roots_lines: Hebrew gedud (H1416) — a raiding band or troop; the wordplay on Gad’s name (Genesis 49:19) and the troops of Job 19:12.
Hebrew gad (H1409) — fortune, good luck; the tribal name, and the deity of Isaiah 65:11 rendered that troop.
Hebrew meni (H4507) — destiny, apportionment; the companion deity rendered that number (Isaiah 65:11).
Hebrew gud (H1464) — to invade or attack in troops; the verb behind a troop shall overcome him.
Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — the heel; the sense of overcoming at the last, at the heel, in Genesis 49:19.
usage: A troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last (Genesis 49:19) — both clauses are the blessing.
By thee I have run through a troop: by my God have I leaped over a wall (2 Samuel 22:30) — exultant strength credited entirely to God.
That prepare a table for that troop (Isaiah 65:11) — not replacing the LORD but hedging the bet with fortune.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon huntian, to chase or pursue game. Webster 1828: to chase wild animals for the purpose of catching or killing them; to pursue with hostility. Scripture’s gravest use of the word has souls, not beasts, for the quarry.
biblical_def: Ezekiel’s indictment of the false prophetesses is the most chilling use of the word in Scripture, because of what they were hunting: Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes, and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls! Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you? (Ezekiel 13:18). They were not persecuting anyone. They were supplying comfort — pillows and kerchiefs, soft things — and the LORD calls the trade soul-hunting. Proverbs describes the same predation in another form: by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life (Proverbs 6:26). The ordinary use is Esau’s: Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it (Genesis 27:5), the errand that gave Jacob his opening. And David complains of a king’s disproportion: the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains (1 Samuel 26:20).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HUNT as to chase wild animals, particularly quadrupeds, for the purpose of catching or killing them; to pursue with hostility; to follow closely; to search for diligently.
webster_full: HUNT, v.t. — To chase wild animals, particularly quadrupeds, for the purpose of catching them for food, or for the diversion of sportsmen.
To pursue; to follow closely; as, to hunt a man from place to place.
To use, direct or manage hounds in the chase.
HUNT, v.i. — To follow the chase; and figuratively, to search diligently, with for or after.
Anglo-Saxon huntian, to hunt; related to hentan, to seize.
scriptures: Ezekiel 13:18

And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes, and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature to hunt souls! Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you?
Proverbs 6:26
For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.
Genesis 27:5
And Rebekah heard when Isaac spake to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it.
1 Samuel 26:20
Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 13 identifies soul-hunting not with persecution but with the supply of comfort, and it is the passage most needed against a preaching that has made reassurance its whole business.
corruption_paragraphs: The women of Ezekiel 13 sew pillows and make kerchiefs. Their offence is not cruelty; it is softness — upholstering the consciences of people God was calling to repent. The chapter has already named the men who did the same thing with words: they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace (Ezekiel 13:10), daubing a flimsy wall with untempered morter. That is the exact shape of the modern therapeutic pulpit, which has learned to speak fluently of a hearer’s pain and hardly at all of his guilt, and which measures a sermon by whether people left feeling better. God’s verdict on the trade is that it hunts souls. The kindest thing that can be said of a man under God’s displeasure is that he is under it, and the preacher who withholds that has not spared him anything.

The second half of Ezekiel 13:18 is the searching question: Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive that come unto you? The two activities are set against each other. A ministry that hunts cannot also save alive, and there is no neutral middle where a man merely fails to help. This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that the law be preached before the gospel — not because it enjoys severity but because a pillow under the arm of a man on the edge of the pit is the cruellest object in the world. Proverbs 6:26 shows the same predation in the seduction of the adulteress, who hunts for the precious life: the word Scripture uses for the soul’s value is the same word it uses for what the hunter is after.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsud (H6679), to hunt or lie in wait for; tsayid (H6718), game or venison; radaph (H7291), to pursue.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsud (H6679) — to hunt, to lie in wait; to hunt souls (Ezekiel 13:18) and the adulteress hunting the precious life (Proverbs 6:26).
Hebrew tsayid (H6718) — game taken in hunting, venison; Esau’s errand (Genesis 27:5).
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — the soul or living being; the quarry of Ezekiel 13:18.
Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue or chase; the parallel verb for hostile pursuit.
Hebrew tapel (H8602) — untempered, insipid; the worthless morter of the same chapter (Ezekiel 13:10).
usage: Sew pillows to all armholes... to hunt souls! (Ezekiel 13:18) — the offence is softness, not cruelty.
Will ye hunt the souls of my people, and will ye save the souls alive? (Ezekiel 13:18) — the two are set against each other, with no neutral middle.
The adulteress will hunt for the precious life (Proverbs 6:26) — the word for the soul’s worth is the word for the quarry.
